newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's next deal likely to be Eurobond issue.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's next deal likely to be Eurobond issue.

text.p: Turkey's next deal in the international capital markets is likely to be a Eurobond issue in dollars or marks, officials and bankers said on Wednesday.

"There is an expectation in the market that Turkey would go for a Samurai issue. But a Euro issue in dollars or marks is much more likely," a government official who declined to be named told Reuters. He did not give an estimate for the size of a possible deal.
Bankers expect the first issue to be set in late August or in early September followed by a second Euro issue three or four weeks later.
Turkey, which has raised around $1.4 billion in the international capital markets so far this year, last issued five-year Eurobonds worth one billion marks in early June.
It also realised a seven-year 500 million mark issue in January, a five-year 300 billion Italian lire issue in February and a five-year $400-million issue in May.
Turkey's initial target was to raise at least $2 billion in the international capital market this year. Officials said the target would be overshot with the next two Euro deals.

"The treasury may return to the Japanese market for a Samurai deal later this year, probably in the last two months of 1997, after strengthening its credibility and winning verbal support from the IMF," a banker said.

State Minister Gunes Taner, responsible for the treasury, and senior economic bureaucrats are expected to tour key financial centres later this month or in September to inform key market players and financial institutions about the change in economic policies and their plans.
The government, which took office at the end of June, abandoned some of the former Islamist-led coalition's economic policies and pledged to increase Turkey's credibility in the international market.
Officials say a stand-by or a longer-term accord with the IMF is not part of their plan.

However, they believe planned measures and their management of the economy will help the government win the Fund's support. This in turn will improve sentiment towards Turkey, which has a B rating from Standard and Poor's and B1 from Moody's, bankers say.
The treasury will service about $3.1 billion of foreign debt in the last five months of this year. It repaid around $5 billion worth of foreign debt in the first seven months.
State-owned Turkish banks have also turned to international bond markets.
The Export Credit Bank of Turkey (Eximbank) launched a $100 million three-year fixed rate bond and a $100 million three-year floating rate note issue on Wednesday.
State-run Emlakbank tapped the mark Eurobond market in June with a 150 million mark deal.
Officials said a plan for a seven-year Euromark issue by leading Ziraat Bankasi had been cancelled by the new bank administration, appointed last month after the change of government.
Bankers say the treasury may tighten its control on state bank borrowing in a bid to realise all public sector foreign borrowing deals harmoniously at minimum cost.
